title: Claude Sonnet 5's introductory pricing ends August 31 — and a new tokenizer hides a second hike
subtitle: The rate card jumps from $2/$10 to $3/$15 on September 1, matching Sonnet 4.6 on paper. A tokenizer change ships 20–35% more tokens for the same text, pushing real bills past parity.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic's introductory pricing for Claude Sonnet 5 ends on August 31. From September 1 the API rate rises from $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens to $3 in and $15 out — a 50% increase on the same call volume. The new rate card matches Claude Sonnet 4.6 exactly, and Anthropic has been framing the change as a return to standard pricing rather than a hike. On paper, Sonnet 5 will cost the same as its predecessor.

The second half of the story is the tokenizer. Sonnet 5 shipped with an updated tokenizer that emits between 1.0x and 1.35x more tokens for the same natural-language input, depending on content mix. Code-heavy and multilingual prompts hit the top of that range. That means a customer moving from Sonnet 4.6 to Sonnet 5 on identical traffic sees the September 1 rate change stack on top of a token-count inflation they may not have benchmarked. Analyses from independent FinOps blogs put the effective per-task cost 20–35% above where the rate card suggests, once tokenizer differences are counted. The list price says parity; the invoice does not.

There is a real product justification for both changes. Sonnet 5 replaces Sonnet 4.6 as Anthropic's default model in Claude Code and the API, and the new tokenizer is part of a broader architecture shift that also delivered improvements in tool-use reliability and long-context reasoning. Anthropic isn't hiding either change — the pricing sunset date and the tokenizer update are documented. What the coverage this week is pointing out is that they combine multiplicatively, and that teams treating the September deadline as a 50% shock will actually see something higher on workloads dominated by code, non-English text, or structured data.

For learners: the practical move if you use Sonnet 5 in production is to run August's tokens through the September rate card and the current tokenizer, and compare against what Sonnet 4.6 would cost on the same workload. Two things fall out of that exercise. First, a real number to bring to your finance conversation, which is not the number on the rate card. Second, a clear picture of whether the capability gain justifies the effective cost — an important habit to build now, because tokenizer changes are quietly becoming a recurring pricing lever across every major provider.
